title: Learning How to Doubt. Part 1
scripture_text: ‘’After Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in the towns of Galilee. When John, who was in prison, heard about the deeds of the Messiah, he sent his disciples to ask him, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect someone else?” Jesus replied, “Go back and report to John what you hear and see. The blind receive sight, the lame walk, those who have leprosy are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is proclaimed to the poor. Blessed is anyone who does not stumble on account of me.” As John’s disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowd about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swayed by the wind? If not, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? No, those who wear fine clothes are in kings’ palaces. Then what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one about whom it is written: “I will send my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way before you. Truly I tell you, among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist; yet whoever is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been subjected to violence, and violent people have been raiding it. For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come. Whoever has ears, let them hear.’’
devotional:
One of the most difficult things a person will ever have to do is to unlearn things. Learning new things is easier than unlearning old things. As Christians we are often put into situations that will demand that we rethink and revaluate what we believe and why we believe it. Often the things that we were taught in the past now don’t seem right, or feel right in the light of our lives and experience. As Christians we will perhaps experience two eventualities; we will meet people who were once strong in their faith, but are now full of doubt and uncertainty, and maybe, we ourselves will from time to time struggle with doubt.

As a young Christian I often received negative teaching about doubt. I was told that I should never doubt, doubt is a sinful attitude, it is a sign of spiritual weakness, it is something that causes God great displeasure and disappointment. When I had doubts I never talked about them, I never told others how I was feeling in case they thought less of me. So I tried to bury them, or ignore them. I often had feelings of guilt and shame, and thought to myself ‘If I really loved God I would not have these doubts.’

This negative teaching is both wrong and unhelpful; it actually makes our doubt worse because it does not encourage honesty or reality. We were never taught what Doubt is, nor how we should manage or respond to it when we experience it.

What is Doubt?

“To be in doubt is to be in two minds, to be caught between two worlds, to be suspended between a desire to affirm and a desire to negate.” Os Guinness.

“Doubt is a state of mind in suspension between faith and unbelief so that it is neither them wholly and is each one partly.” Os Guinness.

Doubt is when your expectations of God and your experiences in life clash, causing fear and confusion.

It is important that we recognise that doubt for the Christian is very different than the doubts of the Non-Christian, in some ways the doubt of a Christian are the opposite of those who are not Christians.

The doubts of most non-Christians are generally painless. When a person who is not a Christian has doubts about God and his love, usually that is a painless experience, because their doubts are not in the context of a relationship. So they have a lethargic attitude towards their doubts, they don’t loose sleep, or get overly anxious about them, it’s not a matter of life and death.

On the other hand the doubts of the Christian are painful because they do have a relationship with God. The Christian has come to love and trust God, they put their hope and life in his, then suddenly a tragedy hits them and their life falls apart. Where is God, this sovereign God who appears to be sitting on his hands and doing nothing? Often the fact that we have faith in God makes our problems seem worse.

The doubts of the non-Christian can possibly harden his heart and make him more rebellious; He may allow his doubts to make him sinister and bitter, pushing him further from God.

On the other hand the doubts of the Christian is often the consequence of a wounded faith. Hard-heartedness or a closed mind does not cause this doubt.

Furthermore the doubts of the Christian are an integral part of his or her growth and if they are handled properly can lead to a deeper experience of God and spiritual maturity. Real spirituality is not possible without honest, healthy doubt handled properly. Part of discipleship is to help people manage their doubts, or to teach them how to doubt properly. In many circles doubt is frowned upon and condemned. There is a false belief that equates all doubt with sin, but this is not the case.
prayer: Father thank you that doubt is part of the normal spiritual process.
